en: Itivuttaka 27:
Ekakanipāta, Tatiyavagga (The Third Chapter)
The Discourse on the Development of Loving-kindness.
This was said by the Blessed One, said by the Arahant; thus have I heard:
"Bhikkhus, whatever grounds for making merit there are that pertain to the acquisitions, all of them are not worth a sixteenth part of the liberation of mind through loving-kindness."
It is precisely through having mastered the liberation of mind that is loving-kindness (*mettā*) that it shines, glows, and radiates.

Just as, monks, whatever luster belongs to the stars, all of that does not equal even a sixteenth part of the moon’s luster; it is precisely through having mastered the moon’s luster that it shines, glows, and radiates—even so, monks, whatever bases for meritorious action there are that are worldly (*opadhika*), all of them—

They do not equal even a sixteenth part of the liberation of mind through loving-kindness; for it is the liberation of mind through loving-kindness itself that, having surpassed them, shines, glows, and radiates.
Just as, monks, in the last month of the rains, at the time of autumn, when the sky is clear and free from clouds...
Just as the sun, O monks, when it rises into the sky, having dispelled all the darkness that has come into the atmosphere,
shines, glows, and radiates; even so, monks,
whatever bases for meritorious action there are that pertain to the acquisitions— all those—

They do not equal even a sixteenth part of the liberation of mind through loving-kindness (*mettā-cetovimutti*); indeed, having surpassed those [other liberations] by means of this very liberation of mind through loving-kindness, it shines, glows, and radiates.
Just as, monks, at the time of dawn during the night, the morning star shines, glows, and radiates; so too does this liberation of mind through loving-kindness shine, glow, and radiate.
“In the same way, monks, whatever bases for meritorious action there are that pertain to the acquisitions,
they all do not equal even a sixteenth part of the liberation of mind through loving-kindness. For it is the liberation of mind through loving-kindness alone that,
having surpassed them, shines, glows, and radiates.”
The Blessed One spoke this matter.
Regarding this, it is said:
"And he who cultivates loving-kindness..."
Immeasurable for one who is mindful;
the fetters become thin for one who sees the destruction of acquisitions.

If one has a mind free from malice toward even a single living being and practices loving-kindness, one becomes skilled thereby; and if one feels compassion for all beings with the mind, [one becomes skilled thereby].
The noble one performs abundant merit. Even those royal seers who,
having conquered the earth with its teeming multitudes of beings,
went about performing sacrifices— [they do not equal him].
The horse sacrifice, the human sacrifice,
the Sammapasa, the Vajapeyya, and the Niraggala—
these do not equal even a sixteenth part of a well-developed mind of loving-kindness.
Even a sixteenth part of that they do not equal,
just as all the hosts of stars do not equal the moon’s radiance—
[that person] who neither kills nor causes to kill.
He does not conquer, nor does he cause others to conquer;
with a heart of loving-kindness toward all beings,
he has no enmity toward anyone.
This matter too was spoken by the Blessed One; thus have I heard.
Seventh.
The Third Chapter.
Its summary verse:
Mind, loving-kindness, both meanings,
merit, and Mount Vepulla.
Intentional lying,
giving, and the cultivation of loving-kindness—
these are the seven discourses.
And the first twenty;
among the discourses on single phenomena,
there are twenty-seven collections.
The First Book is finished.
